Guru Har Rai

Stories of the Sikh Gurus

Guru Har Rai

The Guru of Mercy

In everyday English — the whole story of the seventh Guru

Stories by Eku

How to Read · · BEFORE WE BEGIN

Read it out loud. This story was made to be told. Read slowly, as if you were sitting among family at home — with the smell of the garden at Kiratpur and the sound of the Sutlej river in the background.

The yellow boxes are the characters speaking in their own words. Change your voice a little when you read them — Har Rai's slow and gentle, Hargobind's grave, the Mughal court's stern.

(The purple cues) tell you where to pause, whisper, or raise your voice. They are for the reader, not the listener.

At the end of every part, the green box — Pause and think. Stop there. Ask questions. Let the listener speak. In this story, those questions matter as much as the story.

There are two kinds of things in this book — the bani of the Guru Granth Sahib, which is written down, and the stories of the tradition, told in the sangat for centuries. Where a story comes from the tradition, the book says so plainly — 'the tradition tells us'. Where the words are the Guru's own, the book names them.

Know one thing from the start — Guru Har Rai has no bani in the Guru Granth Sahib. His story comes from the traditional life stories and from modern scholarship. So every great story in this book carries its source with it — what the tradition says, and what history can say for certain.

This book's main story comes from the traditional life stories and modern scholarship. The full list of sources is at the end of the book.

Who's Who · · WHO'S WHO

Guru Har Rai — the heart of this story. Born at Kiratpur, the seventh Guru at fourteen, Guru for seventeen years. The Guru of mercy.

Guru Hargobind — the sixth Guru of the Sikhs, Har Rai's grandfather. A warrior-saint who founded Kiratpur and handed the guruship to his grandson.

Baba Gurditta — Hargobind's eldest son, Har Rai's father. He died before his own father — so the guruship passed to the grandson.

Mata Nihal Kaur — Har Rai's mother. The old writings also call her Ananti.

Dhir Mal — Har Rai's elder brother. He lived at Kartarpur and was close to the Mughal court.

Suraj Mal — Hargobind's son, Har Rai's uncle. He was one of those who claimed the guruship.

Tegh Bahadur — Hargobind's youngest son, Har Rai's uncle. He later became the ninth Guru of the Sikhs.

Sulakhani — Har Rai's wife, the daughter of Daya Ram.

Ram Rai — Har Rai's elder son. He went to Aurangzeb's court at Delhi.

Har Krishan — Har Rai's younger son. He became the eighth Guru at the age of five. Roop Kaur — Har Rai's daughter.

Dara Shikoh — the eldest son of Emperor Shah Jahan, the heir to the throne. Har Rai helped him.

Shah Jahan — the emperor of India, Dara Shikoh's father. Aurangzeb — Shah Jahan's son, who seized the throne and defeated Dara.

Bhagat Bhagwan and Bhai Pheru — Har Rai's preachers, who spread the Guru's message in the east and in Rajasthan.

Phul — a poor boy blessed by Hargobind and embraced by Har Rai. The houses of Patiala, Nabha and Jind came from his line.

Makkhan Shah — a disciple of Har Rai, whose village the Guru visited in 1660.

1 · Birth — Kiratpur · · BIRTH — KIRATPUR

Above the plain of Punjab, in the lap of the Shivalik hills, on the bank of the Sutlej river, there was a town — Kiratpur. Guru Hargobind had founded it — far from Amritsar, a place where the sangat could live in peace.

There, on 16 January 1630, a child was born whose name was Har Rai. His father was Baba Gurditta — Hargobind's eldest son. His mother was Mata Nihal Kaur.

Har Rai was Hargobind's favourite grandchild. Hargobind was a warrior — he had fought four battles against the Mughal army, and even at Kiratpur a great band of horsemen stayed with him. But with his grandson he was quite different — gentle, patient, listening carefully to everything the child said.

Har Rai's childhood passed at Kiratpur — among the hills, beside the river, in the gardens and the sangat. From childhood he was quiet and tender-hearted. He loved animals, he was glad to see flowers, and he could not bear to see anyone in pain.

In 1640, when Har Rai was ten years old, he married Sulakhani — the daughter of Daya Ram. Later they had three children — the elder son Ram Rai, the younger son Har Krishan, and the daughter Roop Kaur.

Har Rai's father, Gurditta, died in 1638 — when Har Rai was only eight years old. After losing his eldest son, Hargobind watched his grandson even more closely — and he knew there was something special in this child.

The date of birth — 16 January 1630

Har Rai was born on 16 January 1630 (Magh, Samvat 1687) at Kiratpur — this date is recorded in the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism. His father Baba Gurditta (1613–1638) was Hargobind's eldest son, and his mother's name was Nihal Kaur — some writings also call her Ananti. Kiratpur was founded by Hargobind in 1634.

The marriage — 1640

Har Rai married Sulakhani in 1640 — also recorded in the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism. His elder son Ram Rai was born on 11 March 1646.

Pause and think — Har Rai was eight years old when his father died — and his grandfather took him close and raised him. Is there someone in your life who keeps you close and, slowly, helps you grow?

2 · The Broken Flower · · THE BROKEN FLOWER

There is a story from Har Rai's childhood that the sangat still tells today — and in that one story, the whole of Har Rai's life is contained.

The tradition says that one day Har Rai was returning from a horse ride. From a distance he saw his grandfather Guru Hargobind sitting in the garden. Har Rai at once got off his horse and ran to pay him homage.

In his hurry, his long robe caught in a bush — and a few flowers broke from their stems and fell to the ground.

Har Rai sat down on the spot — and wept bitterly. To see the broken flowers broke his heart.

Hargobind came near. He consoled his grandson and said —

“Wear your robe by all means — but be careful as you walk. It behoves God's servants to be tender to all things.”

There was a deeper meaning in his grandfather's one sentence — live in this world, live in it fully — but always remain master of yourself. Live without harming anyone.

The tradition says that after that day Har Rai walked with his robe held carefully — and he made a vow that he would harm no one in the world.

Hargobind had seen everything that day. A warrior who had fought four battles saw tears in his grandson's eyes — and understood to whom the guruship should go. The one who can weep over a broken flower is the one who can understand the pain of the world.

The broken flower — the tradition's story

The story of the broken flower is the tradition's — it is recorded in the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism as part of Har Rai's life. Hargobind's words — 'it behoves God's servants to be tender to all things' — are in that same story. This book keeps it here because it was the moment that made Har Rai 'the Guru of mercy'.

Pause and think — One flower broke — and a child wept. Do you think feeling the pain of small things is a weakness — or is it the greatest strength of all? And have you ever felt so much sorrow over a small thing?

3 · Guru at Fourteen · · GURU AT FOURTEEN

The year 1644 came. Guru Hargobind's health was failing. Everyone at Kiratpur knew — the time had come to hand over the guruship.

Everyone in the sangat looked to Hargobind's sons. But Hargobind had decided something else. He called his grandson Har Rai — who was then only fourteen years old.

Hargobind handed the guruship to Har Rai — and in that same year he died. In 1644, at the age of fourteen, Har Rai became the seventh Guru of the Sikhs.

This was not an easy decision. Hargobind's sons were still alive — Suraj Mal, who claimed the guruship, and Tegh Bahadur, the youngest son. But Hargobind chose not his sons, but his grandson.

Of Suraj Mal it is said that he was too caught up in wealth and the things of the world — his heart was not ready for the guruship. Of Tegh Bahadur it is said that he had all the qualities — but he was not yet ready for this work. And Har Rai's elder brother Dhir Mal lived at Kartarpur and was close to the Mughal court — his grandfather had rejected his politics too.

So once again the guruship was decided not by blood but by fitness — as Nanak had chosen Lehna, as Angad had chosen Amar Das, as Amar Das had chosen Jetha. The light of the Guru goes to the one in whom it shines most brightly — whether he is a son, a grandson, or a disciple.

There was bitterness in the family over this decision too — as there always was. Dhir Mal held himself to be the rightful successor, and the Mughal court helped him. But the sangat accepted Har Rai as Guru — and Kiratpur remained his home.

Suraj Mal — why he was not chosen

According to the scholars (and writings based on the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism), of Hargobind's surviving sons Suraj Mal was considered too worldly, and Tegh Bahadur not yet ready. So the Guru made Gurditta's second son, Har Rai, his successor. This decision is recorded in both the tradition and modern scholarship.

Dhir Mal — the elder brother's story

Har Rai's elder brother Dhir Mal lived at Kartarpur. Emperor Shah Jahan had given him land and encouraged the Sikhs to recognise him as the rightful successor. Dhir Mal spoke in favour of the Mughal state and against his grandfather — so Hargobind rejected him and chose his younger brother Har Rai instead. This is recorded in the work of modern scholars.

The date of Hargobind's death — 28 February or 3 March 1644

The sources differ slightly on the date of Hargobind's death — some say 28 February 1644, some 3 March 1644. This book says only 'the year 1644' in the main story, and both dates are recorded here in this note.

Pause and think — The guruship went not to the sons, but to a fourteen-year-old grandson. Is there a right age to become a leader? And does the guruship come from blood — or from a heart that weeps even when a flower breaks?

4 · The Garden of Mercy · · THE GARDEN OF MERCY

After becoming Guru, Har Rai did what was closest to his heart — he planted a garden of medicinal herbs at Kiratpur. Rare herbs were brought from far away — from the Himalayas, from the south, from distant forests.

With the garden he also opened a dispensary — where the sick were treated free of charge. Anyone could come — rich or poor, Sikh or Muslim, Hindu or anyone else — everyone received medicine. Har Rai had ordered that wherever the langar runs, free healing must run too.

Har Rai himself knew the herbs — which herb helps which illness, when a plant should be picked, how a medicine should be made. The tradition says this knowledge had run in the household from his mother and grandmother too — the dispensary was not his work alone, but the tradition of the whole family.

The langar at Kiratpur kept running too — and Har Rai himself ate the simplest food, earned by the labour of his own hands. Whatever valuable offerings came to him, he spent them on guests and on those in need. In the morning he sat in the sangat and explained the Guru's bani, and in the evening the court was held — kirtan was sung, and the Guru's teaching was heard.

There was room in Har Rai's court for animals too — he freed the animals brought from the hunt and made a garden for their care, where birds and animals lived freely. A Guru who wept over a broken flower could not bear to see any animal in pain either.

That is why the sangat called him the Guru of mercy — a Guru whose strength lay not in the sword, but in mercy.

The garden and the dispensary — what is certain

The herbal garden and the free dispensary at Kiratpur are recorded in the tradition and in modern writings as Har Rai's greatest mark. The tradition also calls this garden the Naulakha Bagh — the garden of nine hundred thousand plants — but that name and that count are the tradition's, not a certain reckoning. This book speaks only of the garden and the dispensary in the main story, and the Naulakha name is recorded here in this note.

The simple food — earned by his own hands

Har Rai's eating the simplest food and spending valuable offerings on guests is recorded in the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism. Sitting in the sangat in the morning to explain the bani, and holding court in the evening, are recorded there too.

Pause and think — Har Rai did not raise a sword — he planted a garden. Do you think the world needs a sword to change — or is a garden enough? And where near you is there a place where the sick are helped free of charge?

5 · Dara Shikoh · · DARA SHIKOH

◆ This part is not for younger listeners

At that time the emperor of India was Shah Jahan. His eldest son was Dara Shikoh — the heir to the throne, who loved Sufi saints and Hindu scholars. His younger brother was Aurangzeb — who wanted the throne.

The tradition says that once Dara Shikoh fell seriously ill — the tradition says he had been poisoned. Shah Jahan's best physicians said — now there is only one hope, certain rare medicines that we do not have.

Shah Jahan sent a humble message to Har Rai — could those medicines be found in the Guru's dispensary? Without delay, Har Rai sent the medicines — and with them a pearl, to be ground up and mixed into the remedy.

The tradition says the medicines cured Dara Shikoh. Shah Jahan thanked the Guru and said he would never trouble the Guru again.

When this reached the sangat, the Sikhs asked — Guru ji, why did you help the son of that emperor whose house had persecuted our Gurus? Har Rai said —

“Behold — with one hand man breaks flowers, and with the other hand he offers them — but the flowers perfume both hands alike. The axe cuts the sandal tree, yet the sandal perfumes the axe. We ought, therefore, to return good when we are treated badly.”

But this story did not end there. A few years later Shah Jahan fell ill, and war broke out between his sons over the throne. Aurangzeb defeated Dara Shikoh. Dara fled to Punjab — and came to Guru Har Rai at Goindwal.

The tradition says Har Rai received Dara with courtesy — as one receives a guest. And when Aurangzeb's army was chasing close behind Dara, the Guru posted his own horsemen at the ferry on the river — so that the pursuing army would be delayed and Dara would have time to escape.

But Dara could not be saved. Aurangzeb captured him and had him executed at Delhi — in the year 1659. And from that day, Aurangzeb's eyes turned towards Kiratpur — towards the Guru who had helped his enemy.

The medicine story — the tradition's story

The story of Dara Shikoh falling ill, Shah Jahan sending a message, the Guru sending the rare medicines and the pearl, and Dara recovering, is the tradition's — it is recorded in Macauliffe's 'The Sikh Religion'. Modern scholars cannot fix this help as certain history — Britannica says only that Har Rai assisted Dara 'in some capacity', perhaps by curing him of poisoning. This book tells it as the tradition's story.

The refuge at Goindwal — the tradition's story

Dara fleeing to Goindwal, the Guru receiving him, and posting horsemen at the ferry to delay Aurangzeb's army — this too is the tradition's story, found in Sarup Das Bhalla's Mahima Prakash. Scholars cannot fix this meeting as certain history, but in the tradition it is the greatest example of Har Rai's mercy.

The words about the flowers — the Guru's own words

The words about the flowers and the sandalwood — 'with one hand man breaks flowers, and with the other he offers them, but the flowers perfume both hands alike' — are recorded in the tradition as Guru Har Rai's own words (Macauliffe). This book gives them as his words, in the yellow box.

The end of Dara — 1659

Dara Shikoh was executed by Aurangzeb at Delhi in 1659, on the charge of having turned away from Islam. That is why this part carries the mark for younger listeners — the talk of poison and execution is not for them.

Pause and think — Har Rai saved the life of his enemy's son — and then gave shelter to that enemy's brother too. Do you think an enemy should be helped? And should good always be answered with good — or sometimes not?

6 · The Summons to Delhi · · THE SUMMONS TO DELHI

In 1660, Aurangzeb sat on the throne. He summoned Guru Har Rai to Delhi — explain why you helped Dara Shikoh.

Har Rai thought — going to Delhi is not right. The emperor's heart is not clean. He sent his elder son Ram Rai — who was then fifteen years old — and said — speak the truth, do not fear, and do not take a single word away from the Guru's bani.

Ram Rai went to Delhi. Aurangzeb received him well — and kept him at court. Then one day the emperor's maulvis raised a question — Guru Nanak has written against the Muslims in the Granth. What is that line?

That line is Guru Nanak's — from Asa di Var, on Ang 466 of the Guru Granth Sahib. In it, Nanak says —

Mitti Musalman ki, pei-ai pa-i kumhiar. Ghar bhande ita kia, jaldi kare pukar.

It means — the clay of a Muslim falls into the potter's hands; from it pots and bricks are made, and burning in the fire, they cry out.

In the court, this line was read to mean that Nanak was speaking of the clay of a Muslim's grave — as if the Muslims were being insulted. But Nanak meant something else — he meant that after death, whether Hindu or Muslim, everyone's clay is the same; the potter's clay does not ask whose grave it came from. Nanak was speaking of the oneness of all people — not insulting anyone.

But Ram Rai was afraid. To please the emperor, he said — Your Majesty, this line has been written wrongly. Nanak did not write 'Musalman', he wrote 'beiman' — the faithless. Some ignorant copyist mistakenly wrote 'Musalman'.

Aurangzeb and his maulvis were pleased with this answer. The emperor gave Ram Rai a reward and kept him at court.

But when this news reached Kiratpur, Har Rai's heart broke. He said — no mortal can change the words of Guru Nanak. The mouth that dared to do so, I will never see again.

Har Rai cast Ram Rai out of the Panth — and never let him meet him again, no matter how many times Ram Rai begged for forgiveness. The Guru's bani cannot be bent even before an emperor — that was Har Rai's greatest decision.

The line — Asa di Var, Ang 466

This line is Guru Nanak's, from Asa di Var — on Ang 466 of the Guru Granth Sahib. This book quotes it as it stands in the Granth — 'Mitti Musalman ki, pei-ai pa-i kumhiar'. Its true meaning — that after death everyone's clay is one — is the reading of modern scholars, and it is held to be the true sense of the line.

What Ram Rai did — the tradition's story

Ram Rai going to Delhi, the maulvis raising the question, and Ram Rai saying 'beiman' to please the emperor — this is the tradition's story, found in Macauliffe and in writings based on the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism. Modern scholars (such as McLeod) also say that Aurangzeb had in fact called Ram Rai as a hostage — to settle the account of the Guru's help to Dara. This book follows the tradition's story in the main text, and the scholars' point is recorded here in this note.

Changed or explained — one more telling

Some tellings say Ram Rai did not change the word of the line — he only explained its meaning differently, saying Nanak had meant the 'beiman'. This book follows the telling most stories give in the main text — that Ram Rai said 'beiman' in place of 'Musalman' — and the other telling is recorded here in this note.

When Ram Rai was sent to Delhi

Ram Rai was sent from Kiratpur to Delhi on 30 March 1661 — he was fifteen years old then. This date is recorded in modern writings.

Pause and think — Ram Rai changed one word to please the emperor — and his father turned him away for ever. Do you think that punishment was too harsh? And is it ever right to tell a lie to save the truth — even before an emperor?

7 · The Quiet Years — Kiratpur and the Mission · · THE QUIET YEARS — KIRATPUR AND THE MISSION

Before the summons to Delhi, and after it too, Har Rai's work went on quietly. Like his grandfather he fought no battle — but he kept his grandfather's band of 2,200 horsemen. Peace also needs strength to guard it — and Har Rai knew that.

To carry the Guru's message far and wide, Har Rai founded bakhshishes — centres of preaching. Bhagat Bhagwan was sent to the east, where he founded hundreds of centres. Bhai Pheru was sent to Rajasthan and southern Punjab. And more preachers went out — Bhai Gonda to Kabul, Bhai Nattha to Dhaka, and Bhai Jodh to Multan.

Har Rai himself travelled widely in the Malwa region — where the Brar tribes lived. Hearing his words, many people became Sikhs. The tradition says he also blessed a poor boy named Phul — the same Phul from whose line the houses of Patiala, Nabha and Jind later came.

In 1660, Har Rai made a long journey — he went to Srinagar, and on the way back stopped at the village of Mota Tanda, where his disciple Makkhan Shah lived. Then he stopped at Akhnur and Jammu, where the masand Bhai Kahna received him with the sangat.

By then, trouble was creeping into the masand system too — some masands had drifted from their work. Har Rai tried to set the system right — and gave the care of the sangats to trustworthy, good people.

For seventeen years Har Rai was Guru — from 1644 to 1661. In those seventeen years there was no great battle, no throne seized, no city plundered. Only one thing happened — the Guru's message reached village after village, the sick received medicine, the hungry received langar, and the sangat grew.

The bakhshishes — two lists

The old writings differ on the list of the preaching centres. Writings based on the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism speak of three great bakhshishes — Bhagat Bhagwan (the east) and Bhai Pheru (Rajasthan and southern Punjab) are the greatest names — and also of the preachers sent to Kabul, Dhaka and Multan. Some other writings give a list of six centres — Suthre Shah, Sahiba, Sangatiya, Mian Sahib, Bhagat Bhagwan, Bhagat Mal and Jeet Mal. This book follows the first list in the main story, and the second list is recorded here in this note.

2,200 horsemen — the strength of peace

Har Rai kept his grandfather's band of 2,200 horsemen — this number is recorded in the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism. In his time there was no further war with the Mughal court.

Phul and the journey to Srinagar

The blessing of Phul, and the arrival at Srinagar on 19 May 1660 and the halts at Mota Tanda, Akhnur and Jammu — both are recorded in the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism. The Brar tribes of Malwa becoming Sikhs is recorded in Britannica.

Pause and think — For seventeen years as Guru, Har Rai fought no battle — yet he did not disband his horsemen either. Does peace need strength? And is a Guru's work only to fight — or is planting a garden, giving medicine, and spreading the message also a Guru's work?

8 · The Successor — Five-Year-Old Har Krishan · · THE SUCCESSOR — FIVE-YEAR-OLD HAR KRISHAN

The year 1661 came. Har Rai was only thirty-one years old — but his body was tired. The summons to Delhi and the matter of Ram Rai had broken his heart.

In the sangat, the same question rose again — to whom will the guruship go? The elder son, Ram Rai, had been cast out of the Panth. Who now?

Har Rai called his younger son Har Krishan — who was then only five years old. He placed his hand on his head and made him his successor. The sangat watched — the Guru changed, but the light stayed the same. As one lamp lights another — the flame stays the same, the lamp changes.

On 6 October 1661, Guru Har Rai died at Kiratpur — at the age of thirty-one. For seventeen years he had been Guru — and in those seventeen years he had taught the world that strength lies in mercy, not in the sword.

After Har Rai, five-year-old Har Krishan became Guru — the eighth Guru of the Sikhs. His story is the next book's — and it is a very short story, but a very great one.

The date of death — 6 October 1661

Guru Har Rai died on 6 October 1661 at Kiratpur — this date is recorded in the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism and in the work of modern scholars. He was thirty-one years old, and his guruship lasted seventeen years (1644–1661).

Har Krishan's age — five years

When the guruship was handed to Har Krishan, he was five years old — some writings give his age as five years three months. This book says 'five years' in the main story.

Ram Rai's later life

Ram Rai stayed on at Delhi — Aurangzeb gave him a jagir of four villages in the Doon region, where he founded Dehradun. He remained outside the Panth. This is recorded in modern writings.

Pause and think — Har Rai gave the guruship not to his elder son but to his five-year-old younger son — because the elder son had changed one word of the Guru's bani. Can one word be so great that a guruship is lost over it? And can the truth ever cost more than one's own son?

To Think About · · TO THINK ABOUT

Har Rai's story is not the story of a king, nor the story of a warrior. It is the story of a Guru who became Guru at fourteen, stayed Guru for seventeen years — and in those seventeen years fought no battle.

His message fits into a single word — mercy. Mercy is devotion. The one who feels another's pain as his own is close to God. Har Rai raised no sword, asked for no throne — he only showed mercy, and with mercy alone he gave peace to a Panth.

Har Rai taught that to become a Guru you do not need youth, or strength, or family — you need only one thing — tenderness. The one who can weep over a broken flower can become a Guru.

And the greatest thing — Har Rai said that no one can change the bani. Not the emperor, not the maulvi, not the Guru's own son. The words of Guru Nanak will stay as they were written — even if the price is parting from one's own son.

Har Rai has no bani of his own in the Guru Granth Sahib — but his story lives in every Sikh's heart. He is the Guru who saved his enemy's life, gave medicine to the sick, and did not hurt even the flowers.

After Har Rai came three more Gurus — Har Krishan, Tegh Bahadur, and Gobind Singh. And in the end that light merged into the Guru Granth Sahib — who is the Guru of the Sikhs to this day. Their stories will come in the next books of this series.

But this seventh book ends here — at Kiratpur, on the bank of the Sutlej river, with a question — if Har Rai were here today, in your home, in your city, what would he say? Perhaps this — walk carefully with your robe held close, hurt no one, and answer evil with good.

Where This Story Comes From · · WHERE THIS STORY COMES FROM

Har Rai's bani — one clear fact

The most important fact of this book is that Guru Har Rai has no bani in the Guru Granth Sahib — just as Guru Har Krishan has none either. The Granth holds the bani of Nanak, Angad, Amar Das, Ram Das, Arjan, Tegh Bahadur and Gobind Singh. So Har Rai's story comes from the traditional life stories and from modern scholarship — and every story in this book carries its source with it.

The traditional life stories — Janamsakhi, Gurbilas and Mahima Prakash

The stories of Har Rai's life are found in the Janamsakhis and in Gurbilas literature — above all in Sarup Das Bhalla's Mahima Prakash, which holds the story of Dara Shikoh's refuge. These were written decades and centuries after Har Rai's death, and they hold history and tradition mixed together. In this book, every story of the tradition is told with 'the tradition tells us' and made clear in its own note.

The line from the Granth — Asa di Var, Ang 466

The line in the Delhi part is Guru Nanak's, from Asa di Var — on Ang 466 of the Guru Granth Sahib. This book quotes the line as it stands in the Granth. Ram Rai saying 'beiman', and Har Rai casting him out of the Panth, is the tradition's story, found in Macauliffe and in writings based on the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism.

Modern scholarship

The dates and events in this book were checked against the work of modern scholars — J.S. Grewal, 'The Sikhs of the Punjab'; W.H. McLeod, 'The Sikhs — History, Religion and Society'; Max Arthur Macauliffe, 'The Sikh Religion', Volume 3; the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (Punjabi University, Patiala); and Britannica. Where the scholars and the tradition say different things, this book records both.

One clear thing

In this book, Har Rai is not shown against any religion. He helped Dara Shikoh, who was a Muslim; people of every faith came to his dispensary; and the true meaning of Nanak's line in the Delhi part is the oneness of all people — not an insult to anyone. His message was not to divide, but to join.

The End · · THE END

The story is complete — but Har Rai's mercy is not yet finished.

In the next book — Guru Har Krishan, the five-year-old child Guru, whose story is very short, but very great.

Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki Fateh.
